Meaning

Indices with increasing values; the front is the window minimum
Smaller or equal items before `x` can never be the maximum again
The window is no longer continuous
Validity test using the two extremes (if they differ by at most 2, so do all pairs)
Move the left edge and drop indices that fell out of the window
Every subarray ending at `r` and starting in `[left, r]` is valid

bullets: Time: O(n), each index enters and leaves each deque once.

2762.takeaway: Sliding window with two monotonic deques tracking the window's maximum and minimum; shrink from the left while max - min exceeds 2, and add the window length each step.

The square of the distinct count for this subarray

2913.takeaway: With n at most 100, enumerate every subarray by its start and extend it one element at a time, keeping a set of the values seen.

Checking the whole group with one subtraction
A group is too spread out, so no valid division exists

2966.takeaway: Sort the array and cut it into consecutive triples: if any valid division exists, this one is valid, and only each triple's first and last elements matter.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Add the next prefix element to the sum
Find the smallest value at least `s` that is not in the array
Smallest missing integer from a starting point

p: `6` is not in `{1,2,3,5}`, so the answer is `6`. For `[3,4,5,1,12,14,13]` the prefix sum is `12`, and `12`, `13`, `14` are all present, so the answer is `15`.

2996.takeaway: Extend the prefix while each number is one more than the previous, then walk upward from its sum until you reach a value that is not in the array.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Each turn removes exactly one flower, so the game lasts x + y turns
She takes the last flower only if the total turn count is odd
First player wins on an odd total
That count simplifies to the floor of half the number of pairs

3021.takeaway: Alice wins exactly when x + y is odd (each turn takes one flower, so she takes the last one if the total is odd); count the pairs with odd sum, which is n * m // 2.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: The count of each distinct letter
Only counts matter, not which letter
The optimal minimum is one of the existing frequencies
Letter too rare: remove all of it
Cheapest way to avoid a smaller minimum
`g > f + k: cost += g - f - k`
Letter too common: trim it to `f + k`

p: `word = "aabcaba"` has frequencies a = 4, b = 2, c = 1, and `k = 0`.

3085.takeaway: Try each existing frequency f as the smallest kept frequency; letters below f are deleted entirely, letters above f + k are trimmed down to f + k.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: For each non-empty subset of coins, its LCM (Least Common Multiple) and size
Incremental LCM (`gcd` is the Greatest Common Divisor)
Number of multiples of any coin up to x: add odd-sized subsets, subtract even-sized ones
Number of multiples of `l` up to `x`
`count` is monotonic in x, and `min(coins) * k` is always enough
The k-th amount is at most mid

bullets: Time: O(2^n * n + 2^n * log(min(coins) * k)), with n at most 15.

3116.takeaway: Binary search the answer x; count how many amounts up to x are multiples of at least one coin with inclusion-exclusion over subsets of the coins (using LCMs).

head: Code
Meaning

Number of violating pairs among positions `1..i`
Prefix sums answering range questions in O(1)
Violations among pairs `(l, l+1) ... (r-1, r)`, the pairs fully inside `[l, r]`
No violation inside the range, so it is special

bullets: Time: O(n + q) for q queries.

3152.takeaway: Precompute a prefix count of adjacent pairs with equal parity; a query range is special exactly when that count does not change across it.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Next city after i on the current shortest path (initially `i + 1`)
Current shortest distance from 0 to n - 1, initially `n - 1`
The new road jumps over at least one city that is still on the path
Only then does the path get shorter
Walks the old path from u to v, subtracts one from `dist` for each skipped step, and marks each visited city with `-1`
Cities already removed by an earlier road cannot start a shortcut

p: Why it works: the queries never cross, so the cities skipped by one road are never needed again, and the bookkeeping stays simple.

bullets: Time: O(n + q), each city is skipped at most once.

3244.takeaway: Keep a "next city" pointer on the shortest path; a new road from u to v skips every city between them, and each skipped city is removed once, so the total work is linear.

Shortest path with edge weights 0 or 1
The start cell can itself be unsafe
Cost of stepping onto the neighbour
Keeps the deque ordered by distance without a heap
After the cheapest path, at least 1 health must remain

p: Every cell on this path is 0, so the loss at the goal is `0`, and `1 - 0 >= 1`: the answer is `true`.

head: Path
Cells
Loss
rows: Down the left column, along the bottom to column 2, up, across the top, down the right column

3286.takeaway: A 0-1 BFS (Breadth-First Search with a deque): moves onto safe cells cost 0 and onto unsafe cells cost 1; compute the least health lost to reach each cell.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Bit tricks are easier with zero-based indexes
After operation i the word has length `2^(i+1)`; its second half has `2^i` letters and is the copy
The position is in the copied half of operation i
Map back to the same position in the first half, and add one shift if that operation shifts the copy
Tracing a position back to the origin
The origin letter is `a`, shifted `shift` times, wrapping after `z`

p: `k = 10`, `operations = [0,1,0,1]`; so the 0-indexed position is 9. Going from the last operation to the first:

3307.takeaway: Work backwards: if k falls in the copied second half of a doubling step, subtract the half length and add that step's shift; the total shift gives the letter.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `ans` and `ans + 1` always include one odd number, so their OR is odd; an even target (here only 2) cannot be produced
Clears the highest bit of the trailing ones, giving the smallest `ans`
Constructing the minimum number with a given OR

p: Why it works: adding 1 to `ans` turns its trailing ones into zeros and sets the next zero bit, so the OR fills those positions with ones. Choosing `ans` with the top bit of the run cleared makes `ans + 1` set exactly that bit back.

3314.takeaway: `ans OR (ans + 1)` equals the number whose trailing run of ones is as long as ans's; to make ans smallest, clear the top bit of that run of ones in `nums[i]`. Even numbers are impossible.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: True when two neighbours are the same letter
The word itself is always a possibility

p: A run of length r can be shortened to any length from 1 to r, which gives r - 1 alternatives, exactly the number of equal neighbouring pairs inside the run.
There are 4 equal pairs, so the answer is `1 + 4 = 5`: `abbcccc`, `abcccc`, `abbc`, `abbcc`, `abbccc`.

3330.takeaway: The number of possible originals is 1 plus the number of adjacent equal pairs, because each such pair marks one extra character that could have come from a long key press.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The product is divisible by t (0 is divisible by every t)

p: For `n = 10`, `t = 2` the product is `1 * 0 = 0`, which is divisible, so the answer is `10`.

bullets: Time: tiny in practice, since within a short distance some number has a 0 digit or the needed factors (n is at most 100).

3345.takeaway: Brute force: try n, n+1, n+2, ... and return the first number whose digit product is divisible by t; the answer is always close because a zero digit makes the product 0.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Length of the strictly increasing run starting at i
Extend the run that starts one position later
The subarrays `a..a+k-1` and `a+k..a+2k-1` are both increasing
`a + k` must be a valid index

3349.takeaway: Precompute for each index how long the strictly increasing run starting there is; two adjacent increasing subarrays of length k start at a and a + k when both runs are at least k.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Only one piece: the whole word
The slice starting at i of at most m characters (shorter near the end)
Python compares strings lexicographically, and when one is a prefix of another the longer is larger

p: Why longer is enough: a piece starting at i that is cut shorter is a prefix of the longer one starting at the same place, so it is never larger.

bullets: Time: O(n * m) for the comparisons.

3403.takeaway: A piece can be at most n - numFriends + 1 characters long (the other friends get one character each), so the largest string is the best slice of that length starting anywhere.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Maximum coins when standing on `(i, j)` having used exactly t neutralisations
Path DP with a small resource counter
The better of coming from above or from the left with the same t
Normal case: collect (or lose) the cell value
A robber is here and a neutralisation is available
When the special ability can help
Coming from the state with one fewer neutralisation and adding 0 for this cell
Best over all counts of used neutralisations

p: `coins = [[0,1,-1],[1,-2,3],[2,-3,4]]`. The best route is down the middle and along the right edge.
No route does better, so the answer is `8` (for example, the route through `-1` also reaches 8 by neutralising it).

3418.takeaway: Grid DP with an extra dimension t = number of robber-neutralisations used (0 to 2); at a negative cell either take the loss, or spend one neutralisation to take nothing.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A parity argument replaces a loop
With an odd total the difference is always odd

p: Derivation: left - right = left - (total - left) = 2 * left - total, and `2 * left` is even, so the difference has the same parity as `total`.

3432.takeaway: The difference left - right equals 2 * left - total, so its parity is the parity of the total sum; either every partition works (even total) or none does.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Prefix counts of digit `a` and digit `b`
Window counts as differences of prefixes
One of four parity states of the pair of counts
Encoding two parities in a number 0 to 3
Smallest value of `ca[l] - cb[l]` among left ends with that parity state
We want `(ca[r]-cb[r]) - (ca[l]-cb[l])` to be as large as possible
`a`'s count in the window must be odd (left parity differs from right) and `b`'s even (same parity)
`while r - l >= k and cb[r] - cb[l] >= 2`
Left ends that give a window of length at least k with at least two `b`s (even and non-zero means at least 2); `l` only moves right
Monotone condition, so one pointer suffices
Candidate answer for this right end

p: The best for this pair is `1`, and the other pairs do not beat it, so the answer is `1` (for example `"11222"`: `2` occurs 3 times, `1` twice).

bullets: Time: O(25 * n) (20 ordered pairs of different digits, each linear).

3445.takeaway: For every ordered pair of digits (a, b), a sliding left pointer feeds a table of the best prefix difference for each of the four parity states; the right end then looks up the state it needs.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum cost to clear the array when index `c` is a leftover element and elements from `i` onward are untouched
The two newly exposed elements; together with `nums[c]` they are the front three
Remove the two new ones and keep the carried element
Remove the carried one and `a`, keep `b`
Remove the carried one and `b`, keep `a`
Fewer than three elements remain: remove all at once for the cost of their maximum

p: `nums = [6,2,8,4]`. The first three are 6, 2, 8; the first step has three choices.

bullets: Time: O(n²) states with O(1) work each.
Space: O(n²) for the cache, with a recursion depth of about n / 2.

3469.takeaway: Memoised recursion over (the one element carried over from the first three, the next unseen index): each step removes two of the three front elements and pays the larger.
